set.best_season: Ski ascents run late March through May, best in April and early May when the snow is stable and softens to corn. On foot, July through mid-August is the usual window, while the glaciers are still snow-covered and bridged. From mid-August into September crevasses open wide and Winnie's Slide turns to bare ice.

before.name: White Salmon Glacier
before.fa: Piley, Richards, Thompson — September 9, 1926 (spelling of names unverified)
before.description: Easy snow approach via White Salmon Glacier. Straightforward glacier climb with minimal technical difficulty. Gains roughly 7,500 ft car to car.
gear: Rope for glacier travel and for belaying/short-pitching the steeper sections
Crevasse rescue kit — the route winds around crevasses and outcroppings on the White Salmon Glacier itself
Pickets — Winnies Slide (40-45°, ~6,800 ft) is steep enough that many parties want protection there rather than soloing it
Awareness of late-season bergschrund difficulty crossing onto Curtis Glacier; an ice screw or two is worth carrying for that transition if the schrund is open
hazards: Avalanches off the Hanging Glacier onto the approach/glacier.
Crevasses on Curtis and White Salmon Glaciers, worse late season.
before.overview: An easy glacier ascent/descent on Shuksan's north side, often used as the descent for northside routes and a moderate ski/snow climb in its own right.
before.beta: Grade II glacier route (easy snow), up to 40-45 degree snow. Route to summit via Winnies Slide (40-45 degree snow) or Fisher Chimneys junction. 3rd-4th class scrambling on the summit pyramid. Active Hanging Glacier avalanches. Bergschrunds, crevasses.
before.turnaround: Turn around before afternoon warming increases avalanche hazard from the active Hanging Glacier above the approach valley.
before.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
before.comms: No reliable cell coverage on the glacier or approach valley.
before.descent: Reverse the route; it is the most common descent for northside Shuksan climbs (North Face, Northeast Ridge, Hanging Glacier).
obj_haz: large avalanches off the very active Hanging Glacier into the approach valley
party-induced rockfall in the central gully

waypoints.name: White Salmon Lodge road gate (Mount Baker Highway hairpin)
waypoints.directions: From Glacier, drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 18 miles to the hairpin switchback at roughly 3,500 ft, below the ski area, and park in the small pull-off at the gated White Salmon Road (FS 3075). Parking is very limited and is not allowed on the highway shoulder; do not block the gate. No parking pass is required.

waypoints.name: White Salmon Glacier toe
waypoints.note: Glacier travel begins where the road/approach ends.
waypoints.directions: Walk around the gate and follow the old road past the White Salmon Lodge site for about a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow cover, descend to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the glacier's toe; without it, hold your height through the clearcut and contour, losing elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings, to stay out of the slide alder in the valley bottom.

waypoints.name: White Salmon Glacier
waypoints.directions: Rope up and climb the White Salmon Glacier, weaving between rock outcrops and crevasses. The basin below sits under the active Hanging Glacier, whose avalanches can sweep it, so move through early and don't linger.

waypoints.name: Winnie's Slide
waypoints.note: 150-200 ft step of steep 40-45° snow/ice onto the Upper Curtis Glacier; schrund can be tricky late season.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the glacier among the outcrops to the foot of Winnie's Slide at about 6,800 ft, the only abrupt steepening on this side of the mountain.

waypoints.name: Hell's Highway
waypoints.note: Snow chute connecting to the west edge of the Sulphide Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Climb Winnie's Slide, about 150-200 ft of 40-45 degree snow that can be hard snow or ice late season, onto the Upper Curtis Glacier. Cross the Upper Curtis southward: it starts steep, eases, then loses height to the base of Hell's Highway. Keep the rope tight as crevasses open through the summer.

waypoints.name: Mount Shuksan
waypoints.directions: Climb Hell's Highway, a short chute of steep snow or alpine ice between rock cliffs, watching for a moat where snow meets rock, onto the upper west edge of the Sulphide Glacier. Follow the Sulphide northeast to the foot of the summit pyramid and finish by the central gully on its south face (3rd-4th class) or the West Ridge (4th class).

timing.recommendedStart: Early morning to cross glaciers on firm snow

before.detailed_rack: No rock rack needed for the standard line; carry crevasse-rescue and glacier travel gear.
what_to_bring: extra layers for the exposed traverse near Hell's Highway
pro_tips: This is probably the most common descent route for northside Shuksan climbs, so know it even if climbing something else.
In April the narrowest part of the final summit gully was easier on the climber's left than on the right.
watch_out: Glacier climbing with crevasse hazard present
Early turnaround essential - sun softening increases hazard
In early April a big avalanche debris field can choke the White Salmon creek drainage; budget about an hour to wind through it
before.pro_needs: Glacier travel protection (pickets, screws in late-season ice) rather than rock gear.
before.best_season: Best with good snow coverage, roughly June-August, before crevasses open up late season.
before.approach: From the small pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge on the Mount Baker Highway, walk around the gate and follow the old road past the lodge site for about a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow cover, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Without it, hold your height through the clearcut and contour, losing elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings, to stay out of the slide alder in the valley bottom. Bivy sites sit among the rock outcrops along the eastern edge of the glacier.
before.descent_text: Downclimb the glacier back through Hell's Highway, across Curtis Glacier, down Winnie's Slide, and out around the clearcut to the White Salmon pull-off.
before.bail: Retreat down the glacier the way you came; no fixed bail points.

pitch_detail.notes: From the bivy among the rock outcrops on the glacier's east edge, rope up and climb the White Salmon Glacier, weaving around outcrops and crevasses to the foot of Winnie's Slide near 6,800 ft. The valley below and this lower glacier sit under the very active Hanging Glacier, whose avalanches can sweep the whole area, so move through early and don't linger.

Climb Winnie's Slide, a short, steep snow slope of about 40-45 degrees, roughly one rope length (150-200 ft), until you can step onto the Upper Curtis Glacier. Late season it can be hard snow or ice, when an ice screw or two for protection makes sense. It is often downclimbed in a boot pack on the way out.

Cross the Upper Curtis Glacier southward: it starts steep, eases, then loses height to the base of Hell's Highway. Early on the crevasses are well bridged; by late summer they open wide and the bridges weaken, so keep the rope tight.

Climb Hell's Highway, a short (about 60 m) chute of steep snow or alpine ice between rock cliffs, onto the upper west edge of the Sulphide Glacier. Watch for a moat where snow meets rock. Then follow the Sulphide northeast to the foot of the summit pyramid.

Finish on the summit pyramid by the central gully on its south face (3rd-4th class, steep snow early season) or by the West Ridge (4th class). The gully sheds loose rock under traffic late in the season. Descend the gully, then reverse Hell's Highway, the Curtis Glacier and Winnie's Slide.

access.fees: No climbing fee (Forest Service approach). An NPS permit is required if camping overnight past the park boundary, and it is not free: $10 per person plus a $6 fee, youth 15 and under free.
access.notes: Northwest Forest Pass required ($5/day or $30/annual). No specific climbing permit.
access.rules: Same MBS NF rules as Mount Baker (fire/camping setbacks near named trails/lakes, pack out human waste). Parties are limited to 12 people in the park's cross-country zones around Shuksan.
access.seasonal: The Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) is plowed year-round to the Mt. Baker Ski Area, near where this approach starts; the road beyond to Artist Point is closed in winter.

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for any camp inside the park - quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit at the Glacier Public Service Center (in season) or the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. Camps below the park boundary, such as Lake Ann and lower Shannon Ridge, are in the Mount Baker Wilderness and need only the free self-issue permit at the trailhead.

road.name: Mount Baker Highway (SR-542)
road.status: Paved; plowed year-round to the Mt. Baker Ski Area
road.driveNote: White Salmon pull-off is at a hairpin switchback ~18 miles east of Glacier, just past milepost 51, near White Salmon Road (FS-3075).
road.seasonalGate: Closed by winter snow beyond the ski area

climate.summer: Crevasses open up as the season progresses
climate.winter: Not a climbing season; avalanche terrain
climate.typical: Marine alpine climate, heavy winter snowpack

emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades NP Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount, (360) 854-7245
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth St. Joseph Medical Center, Bellingham, WA
emergency.sheriffDispatch: North Cascades NP SAR (360) 856-5700 ext. 515; after-hours (360) 873-4590 ext. 37; Whatcom County Sheriff (360) 676-6911

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: June to mid-July, while snow still bridges the creek valley and the glacier's crevasses before they open up

May.reason: Firm snow runs from the road-end clearcut to the glacier, but spring avalanche cycles off the Hanging Glacier and basin slopes are still active.

July.reason: Snow recedes from the valley bottom and the clearcut contour gets brushier, but crevasses on the White Salmon are usually still bridged early in the month.

June.reason: Deep snow still fills the creek valley and bridges most crevasses, so the approach avoids slide alder; cross under the Hanging Glacier early.

April.reason: In early April with a deep base the glaciers can be travelled unroped; crampons came out for the Upper Curtis Glacier and the upper part of Hell's Highway, and the snow in the summit gully was firm at midday.

August.reason: The approach becomes a brushy contour with stream crossings, and crevasses on the White Salmon and Curtis glaciers open, lengthening route-finding.

October.reason: Shortening days, first autumn snow over open crevasses, and wet brush on the approach make this a poor time for the glacier.

September.reason: Bare, broken glacier and open crevasses make travel slow and circuitous, and the summit pyramid scramble is looser once snow is gone.

approach_logistics.trailhead: White Salmon Lodge road gate (Mount Baker Highway hairpin)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: At the hairpin on the Mount Baker Highway near mile 52, below the ski area, park in the small pull-off at the gated road to White Salmon Lodge. Don't block the gate.

before.rope_type: single 30m glacier rope (or 60m if combining with Winnies Slide/Fisher Chimneys exit)
before.rope_note: Complex glacier route with short 1-2 pitch snow/rock/ice sections crossing bergschrunds; joins Winnies Slide about 2/3 height. Requires solid belaying and moderate ice technique.
before.corrections: Grade II/easy-snow characterization from the route list is a bit generous — sources describe short technical ice/rock steps requiring real belaying skill, not a walk-up.
rack: Single 30m glacier rope (or 60m combined with Fisher Chimneys exit)

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Lodge road
approach_variants.notes: Small pull-off at the old White Salmon lodge on the Mount Baker Highway. Walk around the gate and take the old road past the lodge site for about a mile until it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the glacier. Without good snow, do NOT go down into the valley — hold your height entering the clearcut and contour, shedding elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings. This is the same decision that governs the North Face approach, and it is the difference between a walk and a fight with slide alder. Going south past Lake Ann and over Austin Pass is not the way parties reach the White Salmon Glacier; the drainage is entered from the White Salmon side of the highway.
hazards: avalanche off the Hanging Glacier across the approach basin
brush in the valley bottom without snow cover
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier
Winnie's Slide holds firm ice when it has melted back
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route proper begins at the foot of the White Salmon Glacier, or from the bivy sites up and right of it. Ascend the glacier weaving between rock outcrops and crevasses; the marker you are climbing toward is the base of Winnie's Slide at roughly 6,800 ft. Winnie's Slide is unmistakable once you are under it — the angle jumps to around forty to forty-five degrees for roughly a rope length, and it is the only thing on this side of the mountain that steepens like that. Above it you step onto the Upper Curtis Glacier.

If you are still on low-angle glacier threading around rock islands, you are below the slide, however long you have been walking. Conversely, if you have topped out on flatter glacier without a steep pitch behind you, you have drifted off the line and are somewhere else on the White Salmon.

approach_variants.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
approach_variants.notes: From the base of Chair 8, traverse downhill into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley and then climb over four thousand feet to near the base of Hell's Highway at the top of the glacier. This is the ski-descent party's usual line in.
hazards: a committing descent at the start that must be reclimbed on the way out
Hanging Glacier avalanche debris across the valley
approach_variants.whyThisWay: Winter or spring on skis, when a party planning a ski descent starts from the ski area base and traverses down into the creek valley rather than walking the old road.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Winnie's Slide at about 6,800 ft is still the reference feature low on the route; higher, the head of the White Salmon is marked by the base of Hell's Highway. Neither is a subtle feature — both are abrupt steepenings out of low-angle glacier.

bivy.name: Rock outcrop bivy, east edge of the lower White Salmon Glacier
bivy.notes: Bivy on the rock outcrops along the eastern edge of the White Salmon Glacier near its foot. Camp here rather than in the approach valley, which is under icefall from the Hanging Glacier.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit
bivy.capacity: Small flat spots among rock outcrops; a few tents

bivy.name: Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
bivy.notes: Camping above the chimneys is what makes Fisher Chimneys a comfortable two- or three-day climb rather than a very long push, and it puts the party above the loose, route-finding-heavy section for summit day. The lower site near the top of the White Salmon is the more common choice and the more scenic; the higher one above Winnie's Slide costs you a steep snow or ice pitch with a full pack. Which is preferable depends on the party and on conditions in the chimneys, and reasonable people disagree. Both are small and exposed, so a party arriving to find them occupied needs a plan.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only in practice. Runoff sometimes appears on the rock below the glaciers in warm conditions, but neither site should be planned around finding liquid water.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — these camps are inside the park, past the signed boundary above Lake Ann. Reserve through Recreation.gov or take a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center within 24 hours; fees apply and the zone carries a small daily party quota. A Northwest Forest Pass covers only the parking at the Lake Ann trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Small platforms for one or two parties at each of two levels — around 6,800 ft where the chimneys top out near the White Salmon, and higher near 7,300 ft above Winnie's Slide

before.name: South Face
before.overview: Once up the chossy gully, find the flake heading up and right and follow it to the crest. Belay from good cracks on the higher slabs. From there, either pitch it out to the top or scramble. Could suit soloing as an alternative to the scramble up the back side.

set.name: North Ridge via Northeast Shoulder
set.approach: Reached from the Tank Lakes side of the Alpine Lakes high route, via the Foss River trails, not from Chetwoot Lake.
set.beta: From the basin east of the peak, climb a wide talus ramp to the nose of the north ridge, then follow the north ridge, over boulders and heather benches, to the summit. Cairns mark the way across the east-side talus; the lower section can be brushy and the path is clear but easy to lose.
set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent: down the north ridge, round the northeast nose, and across talus to the saddle below the Tank Lakes plateau.

before.name: Northeast Shoulder
watch_out: In late July, the lower northeast shoulder has brush where the path is clear but sometimes hard to follow.

set.overview: A long, exposed rock ridge on the east side of Jack Mountain, mostly class 3 and 4 on loose greenstone with up to three short roped steps of low fifth class (the hardest about 5.0). Parties carry a rope and a few pieces for those steps and for protecting the downclimb.

hazards: Three short low-fifth-class steps interrupt the class 3-4 ridge; a party with no rope has no safe way to reverse the hardest one.

before.name: East Ridge
before.fa: Carl Skoog and Gordon Skoog, July 16, 1984 (the same pair climbed a variation of the east-ridge route on September 23, 1984)
hazards: Loose rock typical of the Hozameen Group bedrock
Remote location with a long, difficult retreat
before.overview: A Grade II, class 4 ridge line on the peak's east side.
before.beta: One of Jack Mountain's established routes.
before.turnaround: Use position and pace rather than a fixed hour. The one published timing datum — 9.5 hours from low on the glacier to the summit — tells you this is a full day, so if you are materially behind that pace at the halfway point, reversing the ridge in daylight is the better outcome. Turn around for weather building on an exposed crest, for snow or rain on the loose greenstone, and any time route-finding stalls the party repeatedly.
before.rappels: No fixed rappels. Parties reversing the ridge build anchors on slung blocks as needed; bring tat and a few nuts.
before.comms: No cell coverage on any approach to Jack Mountain or on the peak itself. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB. Nearest staffed contact is the North Cascades Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount (360-854-7245); emergencies go through 911 / Whatcom County Sheriff dispatch.
before.descent: Commonly used as a descent itself. Parties climbing the East Ridge typically reverse it, downclimbing the Class 4 ground with occasional rappels off slung blocks.

timing.recommendedStart: Pre-dawn. The one published figure for this route - 9.5 hours from low on the glacier to the summit - means a full day even before the descent, so start in the dark and plan to finish in daylight.

before.detailed_rack: No published rack exists. For Class 4 on loose greenstone with a glacier approach, carry a 60 m rope, harnesses, a light rock rack (a set of nuts, a couple of small-to-medium cams, and a generous set of slings and long runners for blocks and horns), plus tat and spare nuts for rappel anchors on the way down. Two snow pickets for the glacier approach.
what_to_bring: Headlamp and spare batteries - this is a long day
Map, compass and GPS with your intended approach line loaded
2-3 L water capacity plus a filter
Tent, bag and stove for 3-4 nights
ice axe and crampons — glacier approach
Rope, a few cams and slings for the ridge's fifth-class steps (July)
Sandals or camp shoes for the Canyon Creek ford (July)
pro_tips: Read both published trip reports (2006, up the North Ridge and down this ridge; and July 2025) before you go - they are the fullest public accounts of the line.
The only published timing for this route is 9.5 hours from low on the glacier; treat it as your planning baseline and start accordingly.
This ridge is a legitimate descent option from the north side of the mountain, which is worth knowing if you are climbing the North Ridge or a north-side glacier.
The route is long and very exposed - the difficulty is endurance and exposure management, not hard moves.
As everywhere on Jack, the rock is loose metavolcanic greenstone; a helmet and disciplined party spacing matter more than a big rack.
watch_out: Sustained exposure over a long distance on Class 4 loose rock - a slip is unlikely to be arrested.
Public beta is thin; there is no topo and no fixed gear on the ridge.
The approach involves glacier travel on the east side of the mountain, so crevasse hazard applies before you reach the rock.
Reversing the ridge takes as long as climbing it; underestimating the day is the classic error here.
Weather on an exposed crest with no quick descent is the main strategic hazard.
before.pro_needs: Sparse. Class 4 on Jack's rock is mostly unprotectable, and slings over blocks will be your main protection. Carry enough to build anchors for a retreat rather than expecting to protect the climbing continuously.
before.best_season: Mid-July through September. The Skoog first ascent was 16 July 1984 and their variation went on 23 September 1984, bracketing the practical window. Earlier and the ridge holds snow and the glacier approach is a bigger undertaking; later and fresh snow on the loose rock makes reversal dangerous. SR 20 gates the season, typically opening mid-April to early May and closing late November or early December.
before.approach: Access is from the south, through the Jerry Lakes basin. From the Canyon Creek Trailhead (~1,900 ft, SR 20 near MP 141), ford Canyon Creek and take the McMillan Park-Jackita Ridge Trail #738 to the Crater Mountain trail, continue past Crater Lake, then leave the trail between about 6,400 and 6,700 ft for a saddle at about 7,200 ft. From the saddle, cross the Jerry Glacier and drop into the Jerry Lakes basin, where nearly everyone camps; the route starts low on the glacier on the east side of the mountain, several hundred feet down into the next basin north. Most parties on Jack take three to four days for any route. No turn-by-turn approach exists for the East Ridge itself, so study satellite imagery before committing to a line. In July, from the Jerry Lakes camp a goat path leads to the col; lose about 800 ft into the next basin, climb the southeast arm, cross a snowfield and scramble to the ridge near 7,200 ft.
before.descent_text: The East Ridge is one of the mountain's more reasonable descents — at least one documented party climbed the North Ridge specifically so they could descend this ridge. Reversing it means downclimbing sustained Class 4 on loose rock with big exposure, so carry enough slings and cord to leave rappel anchors on blocks where downclimbing is unattractive. There are no fixed anchors. If you approached from the east glacier, the descent puts you back on the glacier and you should be roped for the crossing. The alternative — descending the South Face and exiting over Jerry Lakes — is a viable escape but leaves you a long way from an eastern or northern camp. Plan and scout the descent before you climb, and leave real daylight margin: the published figure of 9.5 hours from low on the glacier is for the ascent alone. In July the crux was downclimbed on a protected system and only one rappel off an existing tat anchor was needed lower on the ridge; the glacier basin below was best crossed on snow.
before.bail: Retreat off a long Class 4 ridge means downclimbing with occasional improvised rappels — carry tat and a few nuts. The escape options either side of the crest are poor on loose ground, so the honest bail is back down the ridge to the glacier. Once on the glacier, retreat is a roped descent to camp. Bail early rather than late: the ridge is described as long and very exposed, and it gets harder to reverse the further you commit.
before.itinerary: Budget three to four days, the norm on this peak. Day 1: approach and establish a camp on the eastern side of the mountain. Day 2: the climb — the published account records 9.5 hours from low on the glacier for the Skoogs' variation, so plan a pre-dawn start and a full day up and down. Day 3: return. Hold a fourth day for weather; the ridge is exposed and there is nowhere quick to go if a front arrives.

access.fees: No permit fee. Parking at the Canyon Creek Trailhead requires a recreation pass; the East Bank Trailhead does not.
access.permit: Free, non-quota, self-issued Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead register. If you camp at a designated site along the East Bank Trail, a separate limited NPS backcountry permit is required.
access.closures: SR 20 winter closure MP 134 to MP 171. The Canyon Creek bridge on Jackita Ridge Trail #738 was destroyed by a falling tree and must be forded; the creek runs high and hazardous into midsummer.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District - Jack Mountain is in the Pasayten Wilderness. If your approach uses the East Bank Trail, that portion is Ross Lake National Recreation Area under the National Park Service.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass, Digital Day Pass or Interagency pass at Canyon Creek Trailhead; none at the East Bank Trailhead.

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park Complex backcountry permit (covers Ross Lake NRA) - quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. Cross-country climbing camps need a permit for the zone you camp in.

road.name: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway)
road.status: Paved. Depending on the approach chosen, park at the Canyon Creek Trailhead (gravel lot and restroom, near MP 141) or the East Bank Trailhead (roadside, MP 138).
road.driveNote: SR 20 east from Marblemount and Newhalem. The East Bank Trailhead is at MP 138; the Canyon Creek Trailhead is 3.4 miles further east near MP 141, on the left coming from the west.
road.seasonalGate: SR 20 closes each winter between the Ross Dam gate (MP 134) and the Silver Star gate (MP 171), typically late November/early December to mid-April or early May; the 2026 opening slipped to June 14 after flood damage.

climate.fall: September is good - the Skoogs' variation went on 23 September. Dry rock and stable air, but shortening days on a long route.
climate.spring: Snow-covered and best left alone; the glacier approach is avalanche terrain and the highway is often still gated.
climate.summer: The season opens in mid-July, matching the first-ascent date. Expect residual snow in the ridge's gullies early in the month.
climate.winter: Not a documented winter objective; the highway is closed and the route would be a serious expedition.
climate.typical: East-of-crest North Cascades weather: drier and more continental than the Skagit valley, but Pacific fronts wrap around Ross Lake with little warning. The east aspect gets early sun, which helps dry the rock but also warms any residual snow.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North is the nearest named avalanche zone, though Jack lies east of NWAC's observation network.

emergency.notes: No cell coverage. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB. Any rescue from this ridge would be a multi-day operation, so carry enough to survive an unplanned night out.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA 98267 - 360-854-7245; Methow Valley Ranger District, Winthrop, for the Pasayten Wilderness.
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, 2000 Hospital Dr, Sedro-Woolley, WA 98284 - (360) 856-6021, 24-hour ER.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911; Whatcom County Sheriff non-emergency dispatch 360-676-6911. Whatcom County Search & Rescue is dispatched through the Sheriff's Office.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through August, once the Canyon Creek crossing drops and the glaciated east flank is still snow-covered

July.reason: Creek levels fall and the high country melts out through the month; the first ascent was made in mid-July, with snow still on the ridge.

June.reason: Canyon Creek runs high and dangerous with snowmelt, and deep snow on the approach ridges and the east-side glacier makes a multi-day trip much bigger.

August.reason: Stable mid-summer weather, fewer bugs and manageable snow on the east-side glacier make this the best window for a 3-4 day trip.

October.reason: Autumn snow on the loose Hozameen rock and short days make retreat from this remote ridge hazardous; SR 20 closes for winter later in autumn.

September.reason: Low creeks ease the approach, but the glacier turns icier with open crevasses, and fresh snow on the loose rock makes reversing the ridge dangerous.

approach_variants.name: Jerry Lakes and the bench below the east glacier
approach_variants.notes: The East Ridge is most often met as a descent, because parties who climb the North Ridge come over the summit and go down this way, but it is the better of the two to climb and it is reached from the opposite side of the mountain. Access is from the south: the Canyon Creek Trailhead on SR 20 at about 1,900 ft, a ford of Canyon Creek, then the McMillan Park and Jackita Ridge trail gaining some 3,400 ft in four miles to the Crater Mountain trail, up past Crater Lake, and off-trail somewhere between 6,400 and 6,700 ft to a saddle at about 7,200 ft. From the saddle, drop across the Jerry Glacier and down into the Jerry Lakes basin, where nearly everyone camps. Reckon on three days minimum, and note that the summit day begins by losing several hundred feet into the next basin north before any climbing starts. The ridge itself runs about 1,400 to 1,600 ft from its base up to roughly 8,600 ft, where it dies into the Southeast Ridge and a single common crest carries on to the top. Parties disagree sharply about the rock: the lower third is good blocky class three and four, the upper third is fractured and loose, and the published class four understates the ground — a recent party found three short pitches of fifth class, including a wildly exposed 5.0 step in the middle of the crest, and made one rappel lower down off existing tat. There is no other fixed gear, so carry slings and cord.
hazards: Fractured, loose rock on the upper third with almost nothing dependable to protect it
Sustained exposure along the whole crest, with a thousand feet of air below the middle section
The line strays off the crest to the north in the middle third, which is where parties lose it in descent
Only one existing anchor on the route, so every other rappel is one you build and leave
Collapsing snow fingers where the snowfield meets the toe of the east glacier
Long cross-country approach with no trail for the final miles, and 800 ft to regain on the way home
Very remote, with a difficult retreat from anywhere on the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: Jack's east and southeast ridges hold a small pocket glacier between them like a bay, and finding this route is entirely a matter of working out which side of that bay you are on. The Southeast Ridge is the bay's right-hand edge, the East Ridge its left, and the two merge at about 8,600 ft. From the Jerry Lakes camp the day starts by dropping several hundred feet into the basin to the north, then climbing the southeast arm to a level bench at roughly 7,000 to 7,200 ft. That bench is where the mountain's two commonly climbed routes part company, and the decision there is a single either-or. Traverse left and west on scree under the south face and you are on the standard South Face route, whose landmarks are unmistakable once you start seeing them: a small snowfield, then a larger one likened to a fish or a lobster claw, a refrigerator-sized boulder with rope slung round its middle, a stream that only runs in the afternoon, and a short class four step into a hidden chimney. If you are hunting for a slung boulder, you are on the wrong route. Traverse right and north instead, onto the snowfield beneath the pocket glacier, and a few hundred feet of scrambling gains the crest proper. The confirmation is the view over the back. There is a notch at about 7,000 ft on this ridge, and from it the ground falls away onto a big broken glacier dropping north toward Devils Creek; if you can see that, you are on the East Ridge and not the Southeast. The second check is the rock, which low down is good blocky class three and four, where the South Face is loose almost from the start. One trap worth knowing: there are two cols at about 7,200 ft on this trip, the Crater Mountain saddle on the approach and this bench, and they lie four miles apart, so an altimeter alone will not tell you which one you are standing on.

before.overview: Mutchler Peak (7,150 ft; referenced in some older trip reports as 'Snowqueen') is a remote summit in the Buckindy Group of the Cascade River backcountry, part of the rugged, semi-glaciated ridge system southeast of Marblemount that also includes Snowking Mountain (7,433'), Mount Buckindy (7,320'), Mount Misch (7,435'), Bruseth Mountain (7,220'), and Mount Chaval to the east. There is no maintained trail to Mutchler; it sits in roadless country between the Cascade River and Suiattle River drainages and is almost always climbed cross-country as part of a longer Buckindy Range traverse rather than as a standalone day trip.
before.beta: Mutchler Peak sits at the east end of the long southeast ridge that runs off Snowking Mountain, above the Kindy Creek/Mutchler Creek drainage. Parties reach it either by continuing the Kindy Ridge approach used for Snowking's East Ridge (3rd class, Grade II) past the summit and along the connecting ridge/snowfields toward the Buckindy group, or from the south on the longer Green Mountain–Mount Misch–Mount Buckindy traverse, camping at the pass between Kindy and Buck Creeks before crossing to Mutchler. Terrain is a mix of steep heather, talus, snow/glacier remnants, and low-class rock; one documented traverse rappelled over a cornice to reach the peak.
before.turnaround: Given the long, remote approach and the North Cascades' typical afternoon thunderstorm/whiteout risk in summer, set a firm turnaround time to be off exposed ridge and heather terrain by early-to-mid afternoon.
before.alpine_grade: Mountaineers Scramble S4 / Terrain T5 (rated for the Snowking Mtn NE Shoulder portion that this route climbs first)
before.rock_grade: 3rd class (one short step, on Kindy Ridge below Snowking's summit)
before.face: Mutchler Glacier cirque, on Snowking Mountain's southeast ridge
before.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or reservation. This peak is on Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest land, not in the North Cascades National Park complex.
before.comms: Deep wilderness terrain far from any road; no reliable cell coverage should be expected in the Kindy Creek/Buckindy interior. Carry a satellite communicator or PLB.
before.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

waypoints.name: FR-1570 Washout Parking (Cascade River crossing)
waypoints.note: Small pullout for 4-5 cars just past a washed-out culvert, 0.4 mi beyond the Cascade River bridge and 1.9 mi off Cascade River Road (FR-15) at mile 14.2 from Marblemount; FR-1570 is impassable to vehicles beyond here.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road roughly 14.2 miles from Marblemount and turn onto FR-1570, signed for Kindy Ridge and Found Lake, crossing the Cascade River. Park at the washout just past the washed-out culvert — a small pullout with room for four or five cars at about 1,250 ft. FR-1570 is impassable to vehicles beyond this point and the old spur is permanently closed, so the hike starts on the abandoned roadbed near Vee Creek. Cascade River Road access is seasonal and typically gated in winter, and mid-July through September is when the lower slopes are clear enough to be worth the drive.

waypoints.name: Overgrown Roadbed / Way-Trail Start
waypoints.note: The abandoned FR-1570 roadbed (brushy, several windfalls to step over) ends in an old clearing with a firepit, where a steep, unmarked way-trail breaks off uphill toward Kindy Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Walk the abandoned FR-1570 roadbed past the washed-out culvert, stepping over several windfalls including a large log about 0.8 mile in, to its end at an old clearing with a firepit beside a reliable creek, the last easy water before the ridge.

waypoints.name: 4,800 ft Saddle / Kindy Ridge Gain
waypoints.note: The steep boot path tops out at a broad saddle near 4,800 ft, north of Found Peak, where the route gains the ridge crest and a side path drops to Found Lake; footing is loose and the path is easy to lose here in fog or low visibility.
waypoints.directions: From the firepit the unmarked climbers' path climbs steeply at once through old-growth forest on exposed roots, with spur tracks around blowdown and stretches where the tread fades, roughly 2,500 ft up to a broad saddle near 4,800 ft north of Found Peak. The path is easy to lose here in fog.

waypoints.name: Kindy Ridge Climbers' Boot Path
waypoints.note: Point on the shared Kindy Ridge climbers' route used by Snowking/Buckindy parties; the path crosses Point 5695 here, past Found Peak, then drops to a saddle before Mutchler parties head down into the Cyclone Lake basin.
waypoints.directions: Relocate the boot path at the saddle and follow it up through grass and boulders about 600 ft into a meadow with Found Lake below, then continue south past Found Peak, descending the steep path through the cliffs, and climb over Point 5695 on Kindy Ridge.

waypoints.name: Cyclone Lake Basin
waypoints.note: Largest and highest of the alpine lakes on Snowking's flanks; established rough campsites on the benches above the lake serve as the usual base camp for Mutchler's summit push, with reliable water from the lake and inlet tarns.
waypoints.directions: Drop south to the next saddle, then leave the ridge and descend west into the Cyclone Lake basin. Rough campsites sit on the benches above the lake, with water from the lake and the tarns above it.

waypoints.name: Heather/Rock Flank Below Summit Block
waypoints.note: Loose, exposed heather-and-rock slope gaining Mutchler's upper flanks — the Class 3 crux referenced in the route grade; can be slick when wet and is the same terrain used on descent.
waypoints.directions: From camp, head south across the basin and ridge terrain toward Mutchler Peak, then climb the heather and blocky rock slopes onto its upper flank. The heather is loose and slick when wet.

waypoints.name: Mutchler Peak
waypoints.note: True summit at 7,150 ft; open views west to Snowking Mountain's glaciers and south/east across the Buckindy group peaks (Sonny Boy, Bruseth, Misch, Buckindy).
waypoints.directions: Scramble Class 2-3 blocky rock to the summit, with some loose rock near the top.

before.pro_needs: No protection is needed on the standard line: it is a Class 2-3 scramble with no roped glacier travel, and there are no fixed anchors or bolts on the scrambling sections.
before.best_season: Late July through September, once snow has receded from the approach gullies, cliff bands, and heather slopes. Earlier attempts (June) face lingering snow/ice on north-facing terrain and dangerous, swollen creek crossings on the approach. Because of the long cross-country approach, this is usually planned as a 2-3 day trip combined with neighboring Buckindy Group summits rather than a single-day outing.
before.approach: Park at the Cascade River Road washout roughly 14.2 miles from Marblemount, about 100 yards past the Cascade River crossing near the FR 1570 junction (signed for Kindy Ridge/Found Lake). The old FR 1570 spur is now permanently closed to vehicles, so the hike starts on the abandoned roadbed near Vee Creek at roughly 1,150-1,400 ft — parties note the washed-out culvert and downed timber (one log up to 4 ft across) blocking the road about 0.8 mile in. Follow the old road/boot path, crossing several windfalls, to an old firepit near a reliable creek (last easy water before the ridge). From the firepit the unmaintained climbers' path turns steep immediately, threading old-growth forest on exposed roots with occasional spur tracks around blowdown; expect the tread to fade into debris in places — this stretch to the Found Peak area (roughly 2.5 miles, gaining ~2,500-3,000 ft) is the main route-finding crux of the approach. The path dips to a broad saddle near 4,800 ft where the boot path is easy to lose; parties often end up scrambling 300-400 ft above the pass before relocating the trail, then follow it up through grass and boulders (~600 ft) into a meadow with Found Lake below (pools here are not reliably potable). From there the route climbs over Point 5695 and drops to a second saddle before joining Kindy Ridge proper: a broad, mostly open granite ridge combining faint tread and easy slab-hopping, steep but non-technical, with constant views toward Snowking Mountain, Mutchler Peak, and the Cyclone Lake basin. Camps are commonly made near 6,200 ft on the ridge or down at Cyclone Lake (a strikingly turquoise tarn-fed lake); a small stream south of the ridge camp and a tarn just above Cyclone Lake are the best water sources up high. From the ridge/Cyclone Lake basin, Mutchler Peak's summit block is reached by heather and blocky rock slopes rising out of the basin — moderate Class 2-3 scrambling with some loose rock near the top; no published figure gives the car-to-summit distance for Mutchler itself, but Snowking, reached by the same approach over Kindy Ridge, is roughly 16-18 miles round trip. Because the approach is entirely unmaintained (no official trail, no numbered Forest Service trail), competent off-trail navigation is required, and this is a long, full-day-plus approach — most parties treat it as an overnight rather than a single push.
before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down Mutchler's heather and blocky rock flanks into the Cyclone Lake basin, then back up and over the Found Peak/Kindy Ridge saddle system to the 4,800 ft saddle and down through the old-growth/windfall section to the firepit and abandoned FR 1570 roadbed, then out to the Cascade River Road washout. This is a walk-off/downclimb the entire way — no rappelling is involved on the scramble route or its descent. The main descent hazards are route-finding (the boot path through the meadow/saddle area above Found Peak is easy to lose in both directions and there are cliff bands nearby to avoid), loose rock and heather on the steep upper slopes off Mutchler's summit, and fatigue-driven navigation errors on the long unmaintained stretch back to the road, especially if daylight runs short — at least one trip report specifically mentions avoiding a creek-bed shortcut on the way out after dark in favor of staying on the known road/trail line.
before.bail: Descend to the approach drainage and follow it back toward the road.

bivy.name: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
bivy.notes: The base camp for Snowking Mountain and Mutchler Peak, and the standard end of the Kindy Ridge approach. From the lakes the route follows the Kindy and Found ridge crest south-southwest above Cyclone Lake, keeping south of a cornice that overhangs the ridge, then turns west up moderately steep snow to the summit block; the alternative from the east side of the lake is heather and easy slabs up Snowking's east ridge, finishing on the south. Mutchler is the high point of the long curving ridge running southeast off Snowking and is reached along that crest, and the cirque between the two once held a substantial mid-elevation glacier of which only the highest north-facing ice remains. Getting here from the car is around thirty kilometres and two and a half thousand metres of cumulative gain by the time the undulating ridge is done, which is why nobody does this peak in a day. Snow lingers in the basin well into summer, which is when the camping is flattest and the water is easiest.
bivy.water: The lakes, reliable through the normal climbing season. This is the last certain water before the glacier and the ridge crest, and there is nothing running once you are up on the ice.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp back from the shoreline, use a stove rather than a fire at this elevation, and pack out what you bring in. No agency permit is reserved or quota'd anywhere in this zone, which is the practical difference from the park country up the road.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved sites around the small lakes north of Cyclone Lake, room for two or three parties. No toilet, nothing built.

bivy.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
bivy.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

bivy.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
bivy.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
bivy.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

before.name: Mowich Face
before.fa: Dee Molenaar, Gene Prater, Jim Wickwire, and Dick Pargeter (Central Mowich Face); the South Mowich Face was first climbed in 1957 and the North Mowich Face was completed later by a party including Mike Heath, Mead Hargiss, and Bill Cockerham.
gear: Ice screws and a picket or two for the face
Crampons and helmet — the face is exposed to rockfall, so start early and be off it before the sun reaches it
Glacier rope and crevasse rescue kit for the Mowich Glacier approach

Serac and rockfall hazard on the face

Roped glacier travel on the approach — the route drops off Ptarmigan Ridge onto the North Mowich Glacier and ascends it to camp, with crevasses that thin snow bridges can hide. The bergschrund below the face is frequently not passable direct and has to be turned, so budget time for finding a way through.
before.overview: A broad, steep northwest-facing route above Mowich Lake with two named variations. The original (easier) line cuts left around 12,500 ft into an hourglass of snow, ice, and rock, gaining a ledge and then a 40-50° snow ramp to the top (Grade III). A harder variation cuts right instead, crossing a couple of AI2-3 ice steps and 4-6 pitches of 50-60° snow before topping out on the Liberty Cap glacier (Grade IV). Slope angles average about 42° on the lower two-thirds and 47° on the upper third; high on the face there's a windlip/choke requiring a short traverse on firmer snow, and the bergschrund beneath the face can usually be bypassed via a rock band on climber's left.
before.beta: Grade III-IV ice climbing on the northwest aspect; specific documented lines in this area include the separately-catalogued North Mowich Headwall and Central Mowich Face routes.
before.turnaround: Commit only with good conditions; set a firm turnaround
before.face: Northwest side, above the Mowich Glaciers
before.permit: Mount Rainier: climbing on glaciers or above 10,000 ft requires the park's climbing registration; overnight high camps also need a wilderness permit.
before.comms: No reliable cell coverage on the remote northwest side; carry a satellite communicator or PLB.

waypoints.name: Mowich Lake Trailhead (no road access)

waypoints.name: Liberty Cap
waypoints.directions: Follow the Wonderland Trail about 0.3 mile to the Spray Park Trail and climb it through Spray Park past Spray Falls. Where it tops out, go cross-country southeast between Echo Rock and Observation Rock onto Ptarmigan Ridge, leave the ridge near 8,300 ft and drop about 1,000 ft to the North Mowich Glacier, and rope up to the camps at 9,600 to 10,200 ft. Turn the bergschrund, climb the face to the bench near 13,300 ft, and continue to Liberty Cap.

before.approach: From the Mowich Lake trailhead (no public road access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently in April 2025, so the lake is now a long walk in from another park entrance), follow the Wonderland Trail about 0.3 mile to the Spray Park Trail, then take that trail roughly 3-4 miles up through Spray Park, passing Spray Falls. Where the Spray Park Trail tops out and begins to descend toward Seattle Park and the Carbon River, leave it and head cross-country southeast between Echo Rock and Observation Rock, picking up a climbers' path onto the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. Continue up the ridge's lower apron to roughly 8,300 ft, above Observation Rock, then leave the ridge and descend about 1,000 ft of loose rock and old snow to the edge of the North Mowich Glacier. Rope up there and climb the North Mowich (watch for recent rockfall debris crossing the ice) to camps at roughly 9,600-10,200 ft near the Edmunds divide, just below the Mowich Face proper. This is a genuinely long, remote approach with no maintained trail for the upper two-thirds — self-sufficiency and solid navigation are required, and there's no water above Spray Park except melted snow.
before.descent_text: There's no walk-off back down the Mowich Face itself — after topping out, the standard descent is a long carryover, either down the Emmons-Winthrop Glacier to Camp Schurman/White River, or down the Disappointment Cleaver to Paradise, both ending on the far side of the mountain, so arrange transport from there before you start. This is a walk-off/glacier descent, not a rappel descent; no fixed rappels are used on either standard exit. If a party needs to retreat rather than continue over the top, they reverse the approach: back down across the North Mowich Glacier, up and over the ~1,000 ft scree/talus slope near Observation Rock, and out through Spray Park to Mowich Lake, which is a long day/night hike out.
before.bail: Retreat low; the face is hard to reverse once committed

pitch_detail.notes: From the glacier camps below the face (about 9,600-10,200 ft, near the divide with the Edmunds Glacier), stay roped and climb the last of the North Mowich Glacier to the foot of the face. Watch for fresh rockfall debris on the ice: it marks the fall lines coming off the face. Start in the dark so the face is climbed before sun hits it.

The bergschrund under the central face is large and can be impassable late season. It is usually bypassed through a rock band on the climber's left; earlier in the year a snow bridge may go after weaving around the biggest crevasses. Belay the crossing if the bridge is thin.

The lower two-thirds of the face runs at roughly 35–42° on solid snow in good conditions, climbed with running protection on pickets. Near 12,000 ft the surface turns to harder ice and demands more careful technique. The whole face is exposed to rockfall and ice shards; climbing before the sun arrives reduces but does not remove the hazard.

Around 12,500 ft the line splits. The original (Grade III) cuts left into an hourglass of snow, ice and rock, gains a snow ledge around the rock, then a 40–50° ramp. The harder (Grade IV) variation cuts right over one or two AI2–3 ice steps and 4–6 pitches of 50–60° snow. Wrong gullies here dead-end in cliffs; carry screws.

The face tops out on a bench near 13,300 ft; high up a windlip or choke often needs a short traverse on firmer snow. From the bench, slushy sun cups or penitentes lead to Liberty Cap (14,112 ft). The descent is a carryover down the Emmons-Winthrop or Disappointment Cleaver, not the face.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and Ptarmigan Ridge, then up the North Mowich Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Mowich Lake Road is unpaved and seasonal. In a normal year it opens well after the roads on the east and south sides of the park — commonly not until July — and closes with the first significant snow. Since April 2025, though, the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge that carried the only public road to it has been closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers, so Mowich Lake itself is now a long wilderness walk from another park entrance.

From Mowich Lake, follow the Wonderland Trail about 0.3 mile to the Spray Park Trail, then take that trail roughly 3-4 miles up through Spray Park, passing Spray Falls. Where the Spray Park Trail tops out and begins to descend toward Seattle Park and the Carbon River, leave it and head cross-country southeast between Echo Rock and Observation Rock, picking up a climbers' path onto the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge.

Near 8,300 ft you leave the ridge and drop about 1,000 ft of loose rock and snow to the North Mowich Glacier. Rope up there and climb the glacier, watching for fresh rockfall debris on the ice, to camps at roughly 9,600-10,200 ft below the face.

There is no water above Spray Park and no maintained trail for the upper two-thirds of this approach.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun for ice; the face bares out and starts shedding rock as it warms
hazards: Sustained steep ice and snow with multiple line options and no obvious separation between them
Serac and rockfall hazard on the face; the North Mowich crossing collects the debris
A bergschrund that is frequently impassable direct and must be turned

No walk-off: topping out commits the party to a carryover and a car shuttle
Road access on this side has been closed since the April 2025 Fairfax Bridge closure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two named rocks are the only hard markers on the whole cross-country section, and they work in cloud because they are big and they are a pair. You leave the Wonderland Trail and go between Echo Rock and Observation Rock. Not past one of them — between the two. If you can only see one rock, you do not yet know which one it is.

The second thing is counter-intuitive and it is where parties go wrong: at about 8,300 ft you leave the ridge and go down. The face is across the North Mowich Glacier from Ptarmigan Ridge. If you keep climbing the ridge past that point, you are on Ptarmigan Ridge, which is a different route to a different top-out. Losing height off the ridge is correct and is the single clearest signal that you are on this climb and not its neighbour.

The bergschrund is the arrival and it is frequently not passable direct. It has to be turned, so budget time for looking rather than treating the schrund as a formality. Reaching a schrund you cannot cross straight over means you are probably in the right place.

This is the umbrella face, not a single line, and that is the most important thing to carry in. Four separate climbs share this wall and this camp — the North Mowich Headwall, the Central Mowich Face, the Edmunds Headwall, and Ptarmigan Ridge above and to the side of them. They are told apart by which glacier you cross from camp and by what the first ground above the schrund is, not by the walk in, which is identical for all of them. Decide which one you are doing before you leave camp in the dark; there is roughly 4,000 ft of 40 to 55 degree ice and mixed ground above, and being one line out is not a thing you discover early.

What retreat looks like, because it is not the way you came: there is no walk-off from the top of this face. Topping out commits you to a carryover down the far side of the mountain to Paradise or White River and a shuttle back. Backing off means reversing the North Mowich Glacier, climbing about 1,000 ft of scree and talus near Observation Rock, and walking out through Spray Park.

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge bivy above Observation Rock
bivy.notes: Planned camp and the most sheltered ground on this side of the mountain: old stacked rock windbreaks sit here and parties describe it as the best bivy shelter in the area. The catch is position, not comfort — from here you still have to descend loose scree onto the North Mowich Glacier, and parties who camped here have called that descent the inefficient part of their trip. Cross-country zone; permit required.

bivy.name: Edmunds/North Mowich glacier divide camp

bivy.name: High camp below the North Mowich headwall
bivy.notes: Planned camp closest to the base of the face, and the most exposed of the three. Parties who have used it wore helmets in camp because of rockfall and icefall shedding off the deteriorating headwall above; there is no fully sheltered ground up here. Worth it only when conditions are cold and you intend to start on the face within a few hours. Search around 9,200 ft first if the higher ground looks loaded — flat sites there are limited but out from under the wall.

It is more sheltered than the true summit and less wind-hammered than climbers expect, but it is an unplanned option to know about, not a camp to aim for — going there means you are spending a night above 13,000 ft with whatever you carried up the face.

before.overview: Pandora's Box (also called the W Couloir) is the standard moderate couloir linking Colchuck and Dragontail near Colchuck Col. It's a west-facing snow/talus couloir a couple hundred feet east of Colchuck Col, most often climbed as the summit finish for Dragontail Peak via the Colchuck Glacier approach. The couloir is class 3 scrambling with sections of steep snow up to roughly 40-45° in the couloir and about 50° on the snow slope just below the notch on the Dragontail side; it is not a technical ice or mixed climb. A single ice axe, crampons, and comfort on steep snow/talus are the normal kit.
before.beta: From the Colchuck Glacier, ascend to Colchuck Col; the couloir entrance is a couple hundred feet left (east) of the col. Climb moderate snow (up to ~40-45°) to a notch in the ridge. From the notch, drop down and traverse northeast to the true summit — some parties rope up for this exposed traverse. Class 3 scrambling throughout; conditions determine whether it's a snow climb or a talus/scree scramble by late summer.
before.turnaround: Turn around if the couloir's snow is icy/unconsolidated or rockfall is active; this is a moderate scramble with little fixed protection if conditions deteriorate.

before.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly 4.3-4.4 miles and about 2,200 ft of gain (2-2.5 hours). Unlike the Aasgard Pass routes, continue around the lake's west/south side toward the Colchuck Glacier below the Colchuck-Dragontail col. Ascend talus and then the glacier itself - early season mostly snow, becoming firmer neve/ice with exposed talus by mid-to-late season; the glacier's east lobe is generally reported free of significant crevasses but can be hard enough to want crampons and an axe. Climb the glacier to Colchuck Col; the couloir entrance for Pandora's Box (the W Couloir) is a couple hundred feet left (east) of the col itself and climbs to a notch in the ridge. Total approach 3-4 hours. Hazards: firm morning snow/ice on the glacier approach, and the couloir is a fall-line funnel for rockfall/icefall from the terrain above, so an early start to beat sun-loosened debris and softening snow matters.
before.descent_text: From the top of the couloir/Pandora's Box, descend left and traverse northeast to the true summit (some parties rope up for this exposed traverse), or alternatively exit about 30 ft below the notch, scramble Class 4 rock roughly 20 ft, and follow the ridge left to the top. From the summit, the standard descent is southeast to a saddle, then east across a long snow slope to Aasgard Pass, then down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) to Colchuck Lake - stay climbers' left near the granite walls and beware drifting climbers' right into cliffs. Crampons/axe are recommended into mid-summer; early season the descent can largely be glissaded. No rappels are needed on this standard summit-and-Aasgard-Pass finish. If a party instead retreats directly back down the couloir rather than topping out, downclimbing steep snow/ice or building an improvised rappel off natural gear (slung chockstones or horns) in the couloir could become necessary - this specific scenario is not recorded anywhere but is a reasonable contingency to plan for in a steep snow couloir.
before.bail: The couloir can be downclimbed for most of its length; there's no fixed rappel anchor, so retreat relies on downclimbing or an improvised anchor on natural gear.

access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Overnight groups inside the permit boundary capped at 8 people, must camp together at one previously-impacted site, max 14 consecutive days, no re-entry same trip, permits non-transferable. Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.

overnight_permit.what: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (lottery, not free) May 15 to Oct 31; self-issue at the trailhead the rest of the year
overnight_permit.where: Apply in the February advance lottery or the daily lottery on Recreation.gov. The permit names one zone (Core, Colchuck, Snow Lakes, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline) and you camp only there, except a Core permit, which covers every zone.

road.name: Eightmile Road (FR 7601)
road.driveNote: From Leavenworth, take Icicle Road about 8.5 miles, turn left onto Eightmile Road (FR 7600), then bear right onto FR 7601 and continue about 4 miles to the Stuart Lake/Colchuck trailhead (3,400 ft). High-clearance recommended; 4WD advised.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Glacier to Colchuck Col
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — roughly 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft.

This one does not use Aasgard Pass. Continue around the lake's west and south side toward the Colchuck Glacier under the Colchuck-Dragontail col. Ascend talus and then the glacier: mostly snow early in the season, turning to firmer neve and ice with talus showing through by late season. The east lobe is generally reported free of significant crevassing but gets hard enough to want crampons and an axe. Late in the season a band of blue ice can span most of the snowfield, and parties have found a continuous snow finger on the right to get past it.

Allow three to four hours from the lake.
approach_variants.season: May-Jul, best on a firm consolidated snowpack
hazards: Firm morning snow and ice on the glacier — crampons and axe
A blue-ice band across the snowfield late in the season
The couloir is a fall-line funnel for rockfall and icefall from above — start early, before sun-loosened debris and softening snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Climb the glacier to Colchuck Col. The couloir entrance is not at the col — it is a couple of hundred feet left of it, meaning east, toward Dragontail.

The confirmation is what the gully ends in. Pandora's Box is a notch that goes right through the ridge: standing in it you look down the far side, into the Colchuck basin on one hand and the Dragontail side on the other. If the gully you are in simply fades out onto a summit slope rather than opening into a slot you can see through, you are in the wrong feature.

From the notch the summit is reached by descending a little and traversing left, north-east, toward the top; there is also an exit about thirty feet below the notch leading left onto twenty feet or so of class 4 rock and then the ridgeline.

If you have topped out at the col itself with Colchuck Peak on your right, you have simply reached the col and not yet started the route — walk left along the base of the ridge.

climbing_route.label: Couloir from Colchuck Col to Pandora's Box notch
climbing_route.notes: The couloir starts a couple hundred feet east (left) of Colchuck Col, at about 8,000 ft. Climb it to the notch in the ridge beside the Pandora's Box spire. Early season it is firm snow up to 40–45° and steeper near the notch, so most parties self-belay with an axe. By late summer it is loose Class 3 talus. The couloir funnels rockfall, so climb it before the sun loosens the slopes above.

climbing_route.label: Off the notch onto the Dragontail side
climbing_route.notes: From the notch, the ground drops immediately down a steep, narrow snow finger on the south side. A slip here would have serious consequences. Crampons and a confident axe are the norm, and some parties rope up. The alternative is to leave the couloir about 30 ft below the notch, climb about 20 ft of Class 4 rock on the left, and follow the ridge. As the snow melts, an easier way around the finger usually appears.

climbing_route.label: South-side traverse to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Traverse northeast across the easier snow and talus slopes below the south side of the ridge. Then scramble up to the summit at about 8,840 ft. The traverse is exposed in places, so some parties keep the rope on. Afternoon softening makes the snow here slushy, and the descent toward Aasgard Pass leaves from the saddle southeast of the summit.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered
